INTRODUCTION
            Demand No. 77 pertains to the Ministry of Shipping.  The Ministry of Shipping was constituted by bifurcation of Ministry of Surface Transport into two Ministries w.e.f. 7.11.2000 viz., Ministry of Shipping and Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. 
2.         The Ministry of Shipping is responsible for development, formulation and implementation of policies relating to Shipping, Shipbuilding, Major Ports, Inland Water Transport etc.  Besides, the Ministry is responsible for making necessary shipment arrangements by chartering ships at economic and competitive rates in respect of Government owned/controlled bulk cargoes. The main functions of the Ministry relate to Development of Inland Water Transport, Maritime Shipping and Navigation, Development of Major Ports, Development of Lighthouses and Lightships, Shipbuilding and Chartering of Ships.
3.         The Ministry is administratively divided into different wings, namely Shipping, Ports and Chartering of Ships. 
4.         The following subordinate offices, public sector undertakings and other autonomous bodies are functioning under the administrative control of Ministry of Shipping: -
Subordinate Offices:
Directorate General of Shipping, Mumbai,
Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships, Noida, U.P.
Andaman and Lakshadweep Harbour Works, Port Blair and
Minor Ports Survey Organisation, Mumbai.
Autonomous Bodies:
Port Trusts at Mumbai, Kolkata, Cochin, Kandla, Chennai, Mormugao, New Mangalore, Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, Paradip, Tuticorin and Vishakhapatnam,
 Inland Waterways Authority of India, Noida
National Ship Design and Research Centre at Vishakhapatnam and
Dock Labour Boards at Kolkata, Kandla and Vishakhapatnam.
Public Sector Undertaking:
Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Limited, Kolkata,
Shipping Corporation of India Limited, Mumbai,
Hindustan Shipyard Limited, Visakhapatnam,
Cochin Shipyard Limited, Cochin,
Hooghly Dock and Ports Engineers Limited, Kolkata,
Dredging Corporation of India Limited, Visakhapatnam and
Ennore Port Ltd., Ennore.

11.       The Committee observed that in respect of Major Ports, there has been a heavy shortfall in expenditure as compared to the approved outlay for the Ninth Plan. The main reasons for shortfall have been delays in sanctioning the schemes, slow progress of work by the contractors, adverse weather conditions, contractual disputes/litigation, delays in tender finalization, award of contracts and deferment of projects/schemes etc.
12.       The fund proposed for port sector during Tenth Five Year Plan period is Rs. 17416.40 crores. Out of this Rs. 1122.55 crores is expected to be met from budgetary support from the Government and Rs. 5036.93 crores from internal and extra budgetary sources (total Rs. 6159.48 crores). The remaining funds of Rs. 11256.92 crores are proposed to be raised from private funding on lease/BOT basis.
13.       The Committee is not satisfied with the performance of the Ministry of Shipping during Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could utilise only Rs.4838.92 crores out of the approved outlay of Rs. 9428 crores in Port Sector. The Committee is of the view that the reasons given by the Ministry of Shipping for the heavy shortfall i.e. delays in sanctioning of the schemes, delays in tender finalization, award of contracts etc are not of such nature which were beyond the control of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its working and come out with specific remedial measures (predictive and preventive) to eliminate the delays leading to under-utilisation of allocated funds. Agencies/Individuals should be made accountable as and when lapses occur.
14.       The Committee is also of the view that there has to be realistic approach while preparing any Five-Year plan. 44 Major Schemes of Ninth Five Year Plan are likely to spill over to the Tenth Five-year plan, which may affect the physical/financial targets of the Ministry fixed for the 10th Plan. The funds proposed for Port Sector during 10th Five Year Plan period are Rs.17416.40 crores. The Committee hopes that while preparing the 10th Plan, the Ministry of Shipping would have visualized the possible problem and taken remedial action so that the approved plan outlay for the 10th Five Year Plan are utilised optimally.
SHIPPING
15.       In India, there are 102 shipping companies together, which own a fleet of 517 vessels with a GRT (Gross Registered Tonnage) of 7.09 million. Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), the country’s largest carrier, owns 112 ships with 2.95 million GRT, accounting for 42% of national tonnage. The share of Indian flagships in the overseas sea-born trade of the country has been hovering around 30% during the last few years.
16.       Against a target of 9 million tonnes (MT) for Ninth Plan, the achievement as on 1
st April 2001 was only 6.84 MT, which is at par with the target fixed and achieved during the 8th Plan. Thus there has been almost no net addition to tonnage during the Ninth Plan.
17.       The Ministry in their reply stated that the slow progress in tonnage acquisition was mainly due to:-
Difficulty in raising external commercial borrowings (ECB).
Prevailing market condition is depressed and charter/freight rates have fallen considerably, especially in dry-bulk and liner sector.
Considerable changes in the trade pattern, which has compelled SCI to quit many of its projects.
 
TONNAGE ACQUISITION PROGRAMME DURING TENTH PLAN
18.       At the present stage of economic development, India’s liner trade is expected to grow rapidly as there will be increased imports of crude oil, machinery/parts and finished products as well as exports of value added items. According to a study, the liner cargo traffic at the Indian ports would increase from a level of 45.31 MT in 1996-97 to about 118.62 MMT in 2006-07 showing a compound growth of about 10% per annum.
19.       Ministry of Shipping have taken several measures to encourage the growth of Indian Shipping Industry. To facilitate tonnage growth, the Ministry has taken several pro-active steps, viz., implementation of recommendation of National Shipping Policy Committee, abolition of Ship Acquisition Licensing Committee, (SALC) simplification of guidelines for import of ships, doing away the age norms etc.  But in spite of these efforts only 6.932 million GT has achieved during 9
th Five Year Plan.  The Committee enquired about the reasons for failure to achieve the 9th Plan target of 9 Million Gross Registered Tonnage (GRT).  It was informed that lack of conducive fiscal environment has been the main reason for stagnating tonnage and for failure of Indian Shipping to achieve the targeted tonnage of 9 million GRT during the 9th Plan. The Secretary, Ministry of Shipping in his deposition also stated:-
“.....that the most important reason is the lack of facilitative environment in which shipping can grow.... 89 per cent of the world shipping is functioning in nominal tax regime. In India, it is 35 to 38 per cent. Therefore, there is no level playing field for Indian shipping companies. The Committee was informed that a scientific study has been conducted in this regard. According to that study, in an advanced maritime country, the tonnage should be something like four per cent of the value of the foreign trade by way of freight. In India, it is 10 percent approximately of the value of our foreign trade by way of freight. In 1999-2000, our foreign trade was 90 billion dollars which accrued a freight component of nine billion dollars and which is about 450 billion rupees. Indian Shipping Companies are operating at less than 30 per cent of our traffic, which means, 70 per cent of the amount goes to the outsiders. That tonnage helps the GDP to grow. That is why it is very important to develop the shipping industry.”
20.       The Committee was further informed that in a bid to correct the situation further, the Ministry constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri Rakesh Mohan, Adviser to the Finance Minister to review Indian shipping and suggest measures, with the following terms of reference:
To consider the desirability of introducing Tonnage Tax for Indian Shipping.
If found feasible, to work out the modalities of doing his in a time bound manner.
To recommend other fiscal measures necessary to facilitate steady increase in Indian tonnage so that Indian continues to grow as a major maritime power.
21.       The Committee has since submitted its report in January 2002 and has recommended that the government must recognize the role of shipping in the national economy and provide conducive fiscal regime so that Indian shipping can be internationally competitive. In order to facilitate this, Indian Shipping Companies must be given an option to opt for the Tonnage Tax system with effect from the next financial year. Those shipping companies, which prefer to continue to remain within the corporate tax regime, may be given an option to do so. This, coupled with the rationalization of tax regimes for Indian seafarers, would to large extent help rejuvenate the Indian shipping industry, the committee has concluded.
22.       The recommendations of the Committee are pending implementation with Ministry of Finance. However, Ministry of Finance has provided for the following major fiscal concessions:
Section 33AC benefits restored in original form w.e.f. 1.4.2000.
Upper limit of Section 33AC reserves has been enhanced to include general and share premium reserves, w.e.f. 2002-2003.
Depreciation rate for ships enhanced from 20% to 25% w.e.f. 2001-02.
23.
       The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Shipping failed to achieve the target of 9 million tonnes for the Ninth Five Year Plan. The achievement of 6.84 MT is at par with the target achieved during the Eighth Plan. This shows that the tonnage acquisition was static during the Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could not identify the problem of shipping industry during the full five years of Ninth Plan and did not take adequate steps to improve the situation.
24.       The Committee is of the view that the Shipping Industry can play important role in the development of national economy. Therefore, it is necessary to provide conducive fiscal regime to Indian Shipping Sector so that it can become internationally competitive. The Committee notes with some satisfaction the fiscal concessions given to the Indian Shipping Sector and measures taken by the Government of India recently towards growth of Indian Tonnage.  The Committee, however, recommends that recommendations of the Rakesh Mohan Committee should be considered positively by the Government of India and further concessions necessary for the healthy Shipping Sector should be provided as early as possible. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation that Government of India should not levy heavy taxation on Shipping Sector. The Government should explore the possibility of Tonnage Tax régime in the country as early as possible.
 
DREDGING AT MAJOR PORTS
25.       Dredging is the key function of any Major Port so as to maintain adequate navigable depth of the shipping channel.  Dredging is generally classified into capital dredging and maintenance dredging.  Capital dredging is done as part of port development, where as, Maintenance dredging has to be done regularly to maintain the depth of shipping channel. Dredging Corporation of India Ltd. is the premier company set up in 1976 to cater to the dredging needs of the Major Ports of the country on contract basis.  It caters to about 65% of the maintenance dredging needs of the country.
26.       In his deposition before the Committee, the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping explained that the Ministry is facing a lot of problems in respect of dredging. As no budgetary support is at present given to Major Ports for the development and expansion, the capital dredging, to the extent possible are also done by the port themselves, either through their own resources or from the borrowed funds.  However, the ports are not in a position to spare adequate funds for capital dredging. At present, big vessels are not operating in our Ports. As much as 68 to 70% of the transshipment is being done outside the country. Countries like Sri Lanka, Dubai and Singapore have gained at our expense.
27.       In the present age of information and modernization, shipping industry is encountering with the fast changes i.e. increased sizes of ship.  The bigger ships result into a substantial reduction in freight and as such are preferred by shippers.   But these bigger ships are unable to call on indian ports because these ships need greater depth and wider channel.  Most of the Indian ports suffer from draft limitations.  In case the draft is not in improved by undertaking, Capital dredging, the future of Major Ports would be at stake because they will not be in a position to retain their volume of traffic.  Therefore, the capital dredging at a number of Indian Major Ports is basic requirement for the long-term survival of Ports and improving competitiveness of Indian trade. In a developed country like United States of America, the requirement of capital dredging is stated to be made by the state. 
28.       The Committee notes that Major Ports are spending large amount on the capital dredging either through their own resources or from the borrowed funds, which has definitely affected their financial performance.  It is also a fact that for the ports, it is difficult to raise borrowings for capital dredging because it may not result into commensurate incremental resources.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that capital dredging at all the Major Ports should be taken as national priority by the Government of India. The Government of India, as a matter of policy should provide adequate plan funds to all the Major Ports for carrying out Capital Dredging at the Ports.
 
KOLKATA PORT TRUST (KoPT)
(i) Capital Dredging
29.       The Port of Kolkata is situated at the left bank of the River Hooghly and is away from the sea face of the Bay of Bengal by about 105 km. A deep drafted dock system at Haldia is situated at a distance of 40 km from the sea face.  The Port of Kolkata faces difficulty in maintaining its depth due to heavy siltation. The siltation in the river Hooghly and its estuary is continuing unabated mainly due to onrush of sediment from the catchment area of various tributaries and the bank erosional activities persist in the entire Hooghly-Bhagirathi river system upto Farakka.
30.       To maintain the navigational channel, the Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) has to undertake continuous maintenance dredging throughout the year. Maintenance Dredging is, therefore, of prime necessity for the sustenance of navigational depth for the shipping channel leading to both the dock systems at Kolkata and Haldia. The Kolkata-bound channel is for shallower draft and the Haldia bound channel is for deeper draft.

32.       The Committee enquired about reasons for less allocation of Rs. 103.22 crores for the year 2002-03 in comparison to the amount of Rs. 344.43 crores provided last year for capital dredging in Kolkata Port Trust. The Ministry of Shipping in its reply stated that out of Rs. 344.33 crores allocated in Budget Estimates (2001-02), Rs. 341.69 crores was for reimbursement of expenditure incurred by Calcutta Port Trust for dredging and maintenance of river Hooghly and the Haldia Channel (maintenance and dredging) and Rs. 2.64 crores was for meeting the expenditure on establishment of, and maintenance works in, Minor Port Survey Organisation (MPSO). Out of Rs. 103.22 crores allocated in Budget Estimates (2002-03), Rs. 100 crores is for maintenance and dredging and the balance amount of Rs. 3.22 cores is for MPSO.
33.       As per the present policy, the cost on items directly related to dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly as well as the cost incurred on items directly related to maintenance dredging of Haldia Shipping Channel is required to be fully reimbursed to Kolkata Port Trust by the Government on production of Certified statement of Expenditure from Audit. Keeping in view the current provision in the budget, the Ministry of Shipping will not be able to reimburse the entire expenditure incurred on this account by the Kolkata Port Trust. Additional demand, based on the audit certificates will be projected by the Ministry at the time of Revised Estimate stage this year.
34.       The Committee strongly disapproves the procedure adopted by the Government of India in the matter of providing funds to Kolkata Port Trust for Capital Dredging. The Committee is surprised to note that on one side, the Government of India has, in principle, decided to fully reimburse the cost on items directly related to dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly as well as cost incurred on items directly related to maintenance dredging of Haldia Shipping Channel, where as, on other hand, the allocation for capital dredging has been reduced in a arbitrary manner. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be no constraint of funds for the Kolkata Port so far as dredging is concerned. Silting at Kolkata Port is a problem of recurring nature therefore the actual requirement of fund for dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly and Haldia Shipping Channel be identified and provision be made at Budget Estimate stage itself.
35.       In connection with dredging operation at the Kolkata Port Trust, the Committee would like to draw the attention of Ministry of Shipping to the comments made in the CAG report (Report No. 4 of 2002) which are reproduced below:-
“There was short fall of 19.28 million cubic metre (m.cu.m.) of dredging against the ad-hoc targets during 1996-2001 and targeted minimum depth was not achieved despite an expenditure of 1290.95 crore.”
36.       The Committee would like to have clarification from the Ministry about navigability targets achieved vis-à-vis the contracts executed for dredging in Kolkata and Haldia Port. 
(ii) Policy on Surplus Land
37.       The Committee wanted to know whether the Government has any policy for utilisation of surplus land held by the Port Trust. The Secretary replied to the Committee that a policy has been drafted for lease of land on long-term basis by the Kolkata Port Trust for mobilisation of resources.
38.       While appreciating the move, the Committee recommends that the proposed policy of long-term lease of land by Kolkata Port Trust be finalized at the earliest so as to enable the KoPT to moblise the resources to meet its urgent requirement.
 
CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE BUOY MOORING (SBM)
39.       Kochi Refinery Ltd. (KRL) has proposal for augmenting their capacity from 7.5 MTPA to 13.5 MTPA and they have ­­­mooted a proposal for installing a Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) in the open sea outside the port limit for handling the crude oil without utilizing the Cochin Port Facilities.
 40.      Last year also the Committee had gone into the matter. The Committee desired to know the progress made therein. The Ministry of Shipping in a written note stated that no agreement has so far been reached between Cochin Port Trust and Kochi Refinery Ltd. in the matter.  The KRL have not consulted the Port Trust about their requirement for improved crude oil handling facilities.
41.       The Committee further informed that the KRL plans for SBM for VLCC tankers, for which investment required would be around Rs.800 crores.  In this context, it is pertinent to note that the capacity expansion proposal of KRL, is in peril in view of the presence of the private oil companies and for the present traffic of 7.5 million MTPA the crude oil handling through SBM is not likely to be economical in view of the following:-
1.         Extra quantities of inventories have to be kept because of the heavier parcel size received through VLCC.
2.         In the monsoon belt area, tankers handling at SBM are not a proven practice and therefore there is requirement of additional crude oil inventory for the coverage of down times.
3.         For the reliable operation of the refineries, keeping an alternative facility in an adjacent all weather Port is essential as is proposed in similar case of the East Coast Refinery under construction near Paradip Port.  This would call for extra expenditure.
 
42.       The SBM facility is a mono user system and is no way beneficial to any other agencies.  It has also the risk of oil spillage and marine pollution of the area, which has immense wealth of fishing grounds.
43.       The approach and inner channels are the main infrastructure of a Port.  In Port like Cochin, this main infrastructure is provided and maintained mainly at the cost of bulk commodities like crude oil etc. and the facility thus available are used by other industries, which does not have stand alone capacity to provide and maintain this system.  In case the support from KRL is not available for maintaining the channels, the vessels built/calling for repairs at Cochin Shipyard which requires wider channel would be in difficulty.  The industries like FACT, KOMINCO – Binami Zinc Ltd., Hindustan Paper Corpn. Ltd., etc which requires deeper draft for bringing their limited quantity of cargo economically will also be in trouble.  The presence of KRL for sharing the dredging cost of the channels would be a boost and encouraging factor for materializing the ambitious project of Vallarpadam Container Transshipment Terminal which would help economic development of the export and import business the Kerala in particular and of the nation in whole.
44.       Giving the details of the proposals in lieu of Single Buoy Mooring, the Ministry informed the Committee that it is possible to increase the draft at the Cochin Oil Terminal (COT) to an economic level of 14 m, which would enable brining LR-I and LR-II tankers with full load and Suez Max tankers with a load of about 1.2 lakhs tones.  Alternatively, the Port has proposed for developing an inshore terminal South of Puthuvypeen near the Cochin Gut with a tank farm facility at Puthuvypeen and linking the tank farm area to the existing pipeline at COT.  The Port has also suggested that in case the SBM requirement is unavoidable, considering the size of the tankers to be deployed for the economic transportation of crude oil it can be installed off Puthuvypeen with tank farm at Puthuvypeen and connecting pipeline to the COT.  The Port has sufficient land for tank farm construction at Puthuvypeen. The Port has other development proposals like Vallarpadam Container terminal, LNG Terminal Etc. which require about 16.5 meters which is also the draft required for bringing Suez-Max Tankers with full load.  As the channels and marine facilities required are common, the development project will become complementary for sharing the cost.  And hence it would be possible to reduce the oil handling cost further in future when these development projects are materialized.
45.       Apart from land at Puthuvypeen, the Port has land at Vallarpadam for tank farm construction. In case tank farm is located at Vallarpadam, tankers at COT can be emptied directly to the Vallarpadom tank farm and thereafter can be transferred to KRL at a low pumping rate through the existing pipeline, which has capacity limitations due to age. By this arrangement it would be possible to differ the renewal of the existing pipeline in as much as pumping even at very low rate of 2000 tonnes/hour would achieve a throughput of more than 13.5 MTPA per annum.
46.       The port is prepared to take up the development work for increasing the draft to 14m on cost sharing basis. With 14m drafts it would be possible to bring LR-I and LR-II tankers with full load and Suez-Max tankers with parcel of 1.2 Lakhs tonnes. The investment required for this is Rs. 76 Crores. The incremental annual cash out flow including the annualized capital cost is about Rs. 30 crores. Against this it is estimated that a freight saving of around Rs. 70 Crores per annum can be realized from the transportation of 7.5 million tones of crude oil from Gulf area to Cochin in LR-II and Suez-Max tankers. As such a net saving of Rs. 40 crores can be expected when the draft is increased to 14m. The port is also prepared to take up the renewal of the existing pipeline passing through the city up to the KSRTC bus station as a joint project of the CPT and KRL for improvement of the system.
47.       The Port has not received a positive response from KRL for the above alternative proposals stating one or other reasons and they are moving ahead for installation of SBM near Thuravoor.
48.       The Committee observes that despite of alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust, the Kochin Refineries Ltd. is adamant to go ahead with his plan for construction of Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) without giving a positive thought to the proposals. The Committee is of the opinion that both Public Sector undertakings are under administrative control of the Government of India and in absence of agreement, any loss incurred to the Cochin Port Trust will be the loss to the Nation. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 52nd report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) of the Ministry of Shipping and recommends that Ministries of Shipping and Petroleum and Natural Gas should evolve an amicable solution to the problem. Kochi Refinery Ltd. should consider, in the national interest, the alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust before taking up the construction of the Single Buoy Mooring.
 
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
49.       The Ministry of Shipping is responsible for the coordinated development of Inland Water Transport (IWT) in the country and in particular, for the declaration and development of National Waterways. Through Centrally Sponsored Schemes, the Central Government also makes available assistance to the States for developing Inland Waterways other than National Waterways.
50.       Inland Water Transport is generally accepted as a fuel efficient, economical and environment friendly mode of transport. However, the potential of this important mode of transport has not been fully exploited so far. In countries/regions such as USA, Europe, China etc., where IWT Sector was given due importance, IWT has substantial share in inland transport network. However, in India, this sector has not developed with desired pace. Inadequate infrastructural facilities like depth and width required for economic IWT operations, terminals for loading/unloading, navigational aids and IWT fleet are the constraints facing the inland waterways.
51.       The responsibility of development of these waterways rests with Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI). This authority along with Central Inland Water Transport Corporation (CIWTC) as the principle operator are the two Central agencies engaged in the development of inland water transport in the country. The efforts of these organisations are supplemented and supported by inland water organisations of various States and private operators.

INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR)
65.       The Government of India has specific direction to all the Ministries/Departments that the decision of public investment, in any project/scheme, is taken after considering a minimum Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of the proposed projects. Planning Commission insist on minimum 12 percent of Internal Rate of Return for any project/scheme.
66.       In his deposition before the Committee, the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping stated that of late, the cost of funds has gone down which is reflected by reduced rates of interest. With reduction in the cost of funds, there is a need to review the requirement of minimum IRR from its present base level, especially in the case of the Inland Water Transport Sector because of its greater social and economic benefits and the nascent stage of its development. India has navigable waterways aggregating 14,544 kms, of which 5200 kms of major rivers and 485 kms of canals are navigable for mechanized crafts. Inland Water Transport (IWT) has not been able to realize its full growth potential despite being an extremely energy efficient, environmentally clean and economical mode of transport.
67.       The Committee agrees to views of the Ministry of Shipping and is of the opinion that at present Inland Water Transport System in the country is at the initial stage of its development. The allocation of amount for any proposed scheme/project in the field of Inland water Transport Sector is for its infrastructure development. Therefore, there is very low scope for any Internal Rate of Return (IRR) from this Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its approach for Inland water Transport Sector and should not insist for 12% IRR of any scheme/project in this field. The concept of Internal Rate of Return may ever be dispensed with as the benefits from such projects are passed on to the trade and economy.

COASTAL SHIPPING IN INDIA
81.       The Committee informed that presently the cargo moved by Coastal Shipping, which is entirely received for Indian vessels, mainly comprises of coal, klinker, cement, crude oil, PoL and Iron ore. During Ninth five-year plan period, physical target of addition 75 vessels of 0.265 MMT, GRT was proposed in addition to 25 vessels as replacement. 79 vessels have been added to the Costal Fleet during the above period, which exceed the plan target of 75 vessels as “Additional tonnage” account.
82.       The Committee further apprised that although 79 vessels have been added to the coastal fleet the payload capacity in GRT Terms grew only marginally and is lower by almost 200% than the target. This is mainly because a large no. of tugs were added to the coastal fleet having almost no impact on the Cargo/passenger carrying capacity. The pressure on land-based modes, therefore, has not been reduced. Addition to these reasons, the Ship owners are also reluctant to acquire dedicated coastal vessels due to various impediments such as complex customs procedure, time consuming system of Post clearance, high manning scales at par with overseas Shipping, poor port infrastructure etc.
83.       The Committee further informed that for development of coastal shipping, following policy measures need to be considered: -
 
Continuation of cabotage law supported by suitable fiscal and financial incentives.
Earmarking exclusive route for Coastal Shipping along the Indian Coast.
Exclusive berths to be earmarked for coastal ships at all major parts.

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
APPRAISAL OF NINTH FIVE-YEAR PLAN AND PROJECTION FOR 10TH FIVE-YEAR PLAN
The Committee is not satisfied with the performance of the Ministry of Shipping during Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could utilise only Rs.4838.92 crores out of the approved outlay of Rs. 9428 crores in Port Sector. The Committee is of the view that the reasons given by the Ministry of Shipping for the heavy shortfall i.e. delays in sanctioning of the schemes, delays in tender finalization, award of contracts etc are not of such nature which were beyond the control of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its working and come out with specific remedial measures (predictive and preventive) to eliminate the delays leading to under-utilisation of allocated funds. Agencies/Individuals should be made accountable as and when lapses occur.
The Committee is also of the view that there has to be realistic approach while preparing any Five-Year plan. 44 Major Schemes of Ninth Five Year Plan are likely to spill over to the Tenth Five-year plan, which may affect the physical/financial targets of the Ministry fixed for the Tenth Plan. The funds proposed for Port Sector during Tenth Five Year Plan period are Rs.17416.40 crores. The Committee hopes that while preparing the Tenth Plan, the Ministry of Shipping would have visualized the possible problem and taken remedial action so that the approved plan outlay for the Tenth Five Year Plan are utilised optimally.
The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Shipping failed to achieve the target of  9 million tonnes for the Ninth Five Year Plan. The achievement of 6.84 MT is at par with the target achieved during the Eighth Plan. This shows that the tonnage acquisition was static during the Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could not identify the problem of shipping industry during the full five years of Ninth Plan and did not take adequate steps to improve the situation.
The Committee is of the view that that Shipping Industry can play important role in the development of national economy. Therefore, it is necessary to provide conducive fiscal regime to Indian Shipping Sector so that it can become internationally competitive. The Committee notes with some satisfaction the fiscal concessions given to the Indian Shipping Sector and measures taken by the Government of India recently towards growth of Indian Tonnage.  The Committee, however, recommends that recommendations of the Rakesh Mohan Committee should be considered positively by the Government of India and further concessions necessary for the healthy Shipping Sector should be provided as early as possible. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation that Government of India should not levy heavy taxation on Shipping Sector. The Government should explore the possibility of Tonnage Tax régime in the country as early as possible.

DREDGING AT MAJOR PORTS
The Committee notes that Major Ports are spending large amount on the capital dredging either through their own resources or from the borrowed funds, which has definitely affected their financial performance.  It is also a fact that for the ports, it is difficult to raise borrowings for capital dredging because it may not result into commensurate incremental resources.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that capital dredging at all the Major Ports should be taken as national priority by the Government of India. The Government of India, as a matter of policy should provide adequate plan funds to all the Major Ports for carrying out Capital Dredging at the Ports.
The Committee strongly disapproves the procedure adopted by the Government of India in the matter of providing funds to Kolkata Port Trust for Capital Dredging. The Committee is surprised to note that on one side, the Government of India has, in principle, decided to fully reimburse the cost on items directly related to dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly as well as cost incurred on items directly related to maintenance dredging of Haldia Shipping Channel, where as, on other hand, the allocation for capital dredging has been reduced in a arbitrary manner. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be no constraint of funds for the Kolkata Port so far as dredging is concerned. Silting at Kolkata Port is problem of recurring nature therefore the actual requirement of fund for dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly and Haldia Shipping Channel be identified and provision be made at Budget Estimate stage itself.

“There was short fall of 19.28 million cubic metre (m.cu.m.) of dredging against the ad-hoc targets during 1996-2001 and targeted minimum depth was not achieved despite an expenditure of 1290.95 crore.”

The Committee appreciates the steps and efforts taken by the Ministry of Shipping for revival of the Central Inland Water transport Corporation Ltd.  The Committee is of the view that expertise and facilities of ship repair and dry dock facilities at Rajabagan Dockyard should not go waste. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while taking steps for revival of Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd., the facilities of ship repair and Dry Dock available in Rajabagan Dockyard should be exploited fully so that assets and  manpower engaged in those activities are utilised optimally. The Committee also expect that the present ambiguity with regard to future manpower in the Rajabagan Dockyard should be removed and the manpower requirement in Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. for the next five-years be firmed up and informed to all concerned including the Committee. 
The Committee agrees to views of the Ministry of Shipping and is of the opinion that at present Inland Water Transport System in the country is at the initial stage of its development. The allocation of amount for any proposed scheme/project in the field of Inland water Transport Sector is for its infrastructure development. Therefore, there is very low scope for any Internal Rate of Return (IRR) from this Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its approach for Inland water Transport Sector and should not insist for 12% IRR of any scheme/project in this field. The concept of Internal Rate of Return may ever be dispensed with as the benefits from such projects are passed on to the trade and economy.     
(Paras 57, 58, 64 & 67)
 
MARITIME TRAINING IN INDIA
The Committee appreciates the proposal for establishment of an Indian Institute of Maritime Studies under Societies Registration Act, 1960 and placing the Government run Maritime Institutions within the domain of this Society. The move will certainly give a qualitative boost to the maritime training in the country. The Committee, however, recommends that the Government of India may consider to give the status to Indian Institute of Maritime Studies similar to that of IITs’ and introduce a central legislation accordingly at the earliest. 
(Para 72)
 
SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD.
The Committee is not satisfied with the attitude and approach of the Government of India is respect of Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. On one hand, the Government of India has taken decision to go for disinvestment in SCI, whereas on other side, Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. has expansion plan for acquisition of vessels during the year of 2002-03 involving an amount of Rs. 647.84 crores for investment.  The Committee fails to understand as to why the decision for disinvestment of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) has taken place when SCI is able to manage its activities through its own resources.
On enquiry from the Ministry regarding revaluation of assets of SCI, the Committee was informed that no revaluation has taken place, so far, since process of disinvestment started.        
The Committee fails to understand why the SCI has not revalued its assets as the matter of disinvestment of SCI has been under consideration for the last 3-4 years. Owner should be aware of its assets value when a major part of it is being disposed of.
(Paras 78,79 & 80)
COASTAL SHIPPING IN INDIA
The Committee is unhappy to note that during Ninth Five year plan no special attention was given on coastal shipping which is one of the most energy efficient, eco-friendly and cheap modes of transport for movement of bulk commodities over long distances. Considering the vast coastline and congestion on land routes, the costal shipping offers an effective alternative means of Transport. Despite this, no adequate policy measures have been taken by the Ministry. There are 184 minor/intermediate ports in the country along the 5560 kms coastline of India. Minor/intermediate ports can play important role in the coastal Shipping. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Shipping should frame a comprehensive policy and prepare plans to promote the coastal shipping in the country. 
(Para 84)
